rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Turn 3 Game End 4 Big Mountain Expansion Overview Race your goats up the mountains as many times as you can while trying to scale as many different mountains as you can. Turn Roll the 4 dice. If more than one die is a 1, you can turn the extra 1s into any number you wish, but must finish adjustments with at least one 1 showing. Sort the dice into group(s) of your choosing. Each group that sums to a value between 5 and 10 moves your goat on that track; any that sum outside this does nothing. Multiple goats can share the same space, except at the top of the mountain. When a player moves a goat to the top of a mountain, they take a Point Token (shown next to the mountain number at the top of the mountain) from that mountain (if available), and return any goat already there to the foot of the mountain, leaving their goat at the top. If a player creates a grouping of dice that would move a goat up a mountain, but their goat is already at the top, they instead claim one Point Token from this mountain's supply (if available). When a player has collected a point token from every mountain, they claim the highest bonus token (shown above the point tokens). This can be done multiple times - each time you make a new set of all mountains. Game End When the Bonus Token pile runs out, or THREE Mountains run out of normal tokens, finish the current round. Count up your Mountain and Bonus Tokens, the player with the most points, wins! If tied, the tied player with the most goats currently on mountain tops wins! If still tied, the tied player with the goat on the highest valued mountain top wins! Big Mountain Expansion In the Big Mountain expansion, goats ascend a single-file path with only the highest climbers earning points. Players must choose between battling for the regular mountains or risking the Big Mountain where timing is crucial . To place, you select a sum between 11-24 and put a goat on the corresponding Big Mountain spot, sacrificing your ability to score on the regular mountain tracks. You can however, move goats back and forth between the Big Mountain and regular ones during the game. At the end of the game, points are awarded based on the number and ranking of your goats on the Big Mountain. In 2-player games, the points are 12/8/4 In 3-player games, 16/12/8/4 In 4- or 5-player games, 15/12/9/6/3 Players can score multiple times if they have goats in qualifying spots. For example, at the end of a 2-player game, if you have a goat on the 23 spot and the 16 spot and your opponent has a goat on the 21 spot, you will get 16 points (12+4) and your opponent will get 8 points. This expansion gives you more choices as you are now able to move goats to the Big Mountain when there are no more point tokens available at the top of the regular mountains.

[Rating: 1/10] Update: Sept 2021  Went flat very fast  ---------------------------  A better and slightly more interactive push-your-luck game than Can't Stop. I would rather just play this than Can't Stop

[Rating: 1/10] I never expected Can't Stop as a point salad game. Here the spaces are limited and never blocked, but you can't get extra turns either. No highs, no lows. Only efficiency remains. And then you get rewarded for going wide with those bonus points. I thought "ok surely those point tokens change in order, to reward going early or late or whatever" but nah. Eventually a column run out of points and people have no reason to go there, so it's not like the tightening stakes of Can't Stop either.

[Rating: 2/10] Reasonably fun game of chicken, though when compared to something like, e.g., CAN'T STOP, you begin to crave the much larger push-your-luck mechanism that’s clearly missing here. The aim is more about timing—knowing if/when to push to the top of a mountain or wait for an opponent to do it first so you have a chance to knock them down the very next turn and assume their position with less of an immediate threat. But the decision space is (obviously) small, and small decision spaces only work when the player is taking a greater risk. It does have the advantage of being teachable and playable in 

[Rating: 2/10] A very unappealing iteration of Can't Stop that removes the push-your-luck element and instead just dividing up dice each turn to climb up the various-length tracks. There's a little to think about in trying to knock opponents off the top of mountains to stop them sitting there and repeatedly collecting the column's scoring token, but ultimately it manages to feel clearly iterative of Can't Stop without actually improving anything and whilst removing a lot of immediacy and drama, which are then sorely missed.

[Rating: 2/10] This game makes you feel like you're making a choice, but you mostly aren't. All you can do is hope for good numbers, and move your goats accordingly.  The score system isn't interesting either. If you get many tiles of the same number, the others are supposed to counter that by collecting various types of tiles to get the set bonus. Guess what, you got all(or most) the tiles of a single number, so they can't complete a set! You might think you have a choice to wait before the last space, but just moving up is almost always better. +1.0 easy setup, short playtime

[Rating: 3/10] Online: variant of Can't Stop lacking the original exciting climb to the top as Level X replaces it with collecting numerical tokens and followed by anticlimactic addition at game end. First time I can say I've been turned off by a die roller, especially online.

[Rating: 3/10] It's an okay-ish game, but would not play it again. There are many more interesting games out there.

[Rating: 3/10] Not groundbreaking, will play at different player counts and see if it is more interesting than 2pl

[Rating: 3/10] Literally a roll and move - now with tracks. The teensiest decision ever to make on your turn you wonder why you're even playing it.
